title: Pricing the Choice of Architecture
summary: Work through Pricing the Choice of Architecture.

sections: When a bounded loop beats a single call

blocks.md: This lesson follows **Pricing the Choice of Architecture** in *Agent Economics* (Vol III).

blocks.source: Vol III, Agent Economics, § Pricing the Choice of Architecture
blocks.md: A spending bound makes a proposed architecture admissible under its budget, but cost per accepted task determines whether it is worth deploying. When choosing among deterministic code, a fixed model-assisted workflow, a bounded loop, and multi-agent delegation, system architects often frame the decision as an ideological debate between programmatic control and model autonomy. In production systems engineering, however, this decision is an empirical optimization problem governed by an acceptance contract.

questions.q: The section **Pricing the Choice of Architecture** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: Measured cost per accepted task is the sum of every initiated task's account, each charge in exactly one category, divided by the distinct tasks accepted under one declared contract.

Accepted tasks per unit time is the platform's deliverable, so sustaining goodput G at acceptance alpha requires admitting G/alpha trajectories and any change that lowers acceptance raises offered load.

Ideal prefix reuse bills the quadratic re-send at the cached rate, which lowers its coefficient without removing it, so a compaction pays back only after enough turns to recover its rewrite and lost cache.

Every budget account in the tree keeps budget = settled + reserved + free under atomic, logged transitions, so a delegation tree conserves spending and a stopped child keeps its reservation until its late bills settle.
